rows.subtopic: Domains, Ranges and Principal Value Branches
rows.figure: REQUIRED - the stem is only 'The following graph represents :'; the curve (horizontal asymptotes y = pi as x -> -infinity and y = 0 as x -> +infinity, crossing the y-axis at (0, pi/2)) IS the question. Page idx 2.
rows.solution:
Read the three features the printed curve shows: it is defined for every real x, it decreases steadily from the horizontal asymptote \(y = \pi\) on the far left to the horizontal asymptote \(y = 0\) on the far right, and it cuts the y-axis at \(\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\).

Test each choice against those. The graph of \(y = \tan^{-1} x\) is INCREASING, running from \(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) to \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), so it is ruled out both by the direction and by the asymptotes. The graphs of \(y = \sec^{-1} x\) and \(y = \operatorname{cosec}^{-1} x\) are not defined for \(-1 < x < 1\), so neither can be a single unbroken curve crossing the y-axis at all. Only \(y = \cot^{-1} x\) has domain R with range \((0, \pi)\); it decreases throughout, \(\cot^{-1} x \to \pi\) as \(x \to -\infty\), \(\cot^{-1} x \to 0\) as \(x \to \infty\), and \(\cot^{-1} 0 = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), matching the marked point exactly. Hence the graph represents option (B) \(y = \cot^{-1} x\).

rows.stem: Let \(A = [a_{ij}]\) be a \(2 \times 2\) matrix whose elements are given by \(a_{ij} = \dfrac{(2i - j)^2}{3}\). Then \(A'\) is :
rows.solution:
Build A entry by entry from \(a_{ij} = \dfrac{(2i - j)^2}{3}\). For \(i = 1\): \(a_{11} = \dfrac{(2 - 1)^2}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3}\) and \(a_{12} = \dfrac{(2 - 2)^2}{3} = 0\). For \(i = 2\): \(a_{21} = \dfrac{(4 - 1)^2}{3} = \dfrac{9}{3} = 3\) and \(a_{22} = \dfrac{(4 - 2)^2}{3} = \dfrac{4}{3}\).

So \(A = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 3 & \frac{4}{3} \end{bmatrix}\), and the transpose interchanges rows and columns, giving \(A' = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{3} & 3 \\ 0 & \frac{4}{3} \end{bmatrix}\). Note that A itself, not its transpose, is the choice with 0 in the top right — a common slip. Hence the answer is option (A) \(\begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{3} & 3 \\ 0 & \frac{4}{3} \end{bmatrix}\).

rows.stem: If the distance travelled by a particle in t seconds is given by \(S = 72t + 3t^2 - t^3\), then time taken by the particle to come to rest is :
rows.solution:
The particle is at rest when its velocity is zero, and velocity is the derivative of distance with respect to time. From \(S = 72t + 3t^2 - t^3\), \(v = \dfrac{dS}{dt} = 72 + 6t - 3t^2\).

Setting \(v = 0\) gives \(3t^2 - 6t - 72 = 0\), that is \(t^2 - 2t - 24 = 0\), which factorises as \((t - 6)(t + 4) = 0\). The roots are \(t = 6\) and \(t = -4\), and a negative time is rejected. Hence the particle comes to rest after 6 seconds, which is option (B) 6 seconds.

rows.subtopic: Order and Degree of a Differential Equation
rows.stem: The sum of the order and the degree of the differential equation \(4\left[\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\right]^2 + 3\left[1 + \left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^2 - y\right] = 0\) is :
rows.solution:
The equation is \(4\left[\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\right]^2 + 3\left[1 + \left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^2 - y\right] = 0\), which is already a polynomial in the derivatives.

The ORDER is the order of the highest derivative present, here \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\), so the order is 2. The DEGREE is the power to which that highest-order derivative is raised once the equation is polynomial in the derivatives; here \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) appears squared, so the degree is 2. (The square on \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) is irrelevant to the degree — only the highest-order derivative counts.)

Hence the sum is \(2 + 2 = 4\), which is option (D) \(4\).

rows.stem: The probability that it will rain tomorrow in cities A, B and C is 60%, 70% and 80% respectively. The probability that it will rain tomorrow in at least one of the cities is :
rows.solution:
Take the three cities' weather to be independent, as the chapter intends. The probabilities of rain are \(P(A) = \dfrac{6}{10}\), \(P(B) = \dfrac{7}{10}\) and \(P(C) = \dfrac{8}{10}\), so the probabilities of no rain are \(\dfrac{4}{10}\), \(\dfrac{3}{10}\) and \(\dfrac{2}{10}\).

"At least one" is the complement of "none", which is much the quicker route. The probability that it rains in none of the three cities is \(\dfrac{4}{10} \times \dfrac{3}{10} \times \dfrac{2}{10} = \dfrac{24}{1000} = \dfrac{6}{250}\).

Hence the probability of rain in at least one city is \(1 - \dfrac{6}{250} = \dfrac{244}{250}\), which is option (B) \(\dfrac{244}{250}\). (As a sanity check this is \(0.976\), which is properly less than 1 — the choice 1 would say rain somewhere is certain, which it is not.)

rows.stem: Find the interval(s) in which the function \(f(x) = \dfrac{x}{\log x}\), where \(x \in (0, 1) \cup (1, \infty)\), is increasing.
rows.solution:
Differentiate by the quotient rule: with \(f(x) = \dfrac{x}{\log x}\),
\(f'(x) = \dfrac{\log x \cdot 1 - x \cdot \frac{1}{x}}{(\log x)^2} = \dfrac{\log x - 1}{(\log x)^2}\).

The denominator \((\log x)^2\) is positive throughout the given domain \((0, 1) \cup (1, \infty)\), so the sign of \(f'\) is the sign of \(\log x - 1\). This is positive exactly when \(\log x > 1\), that is \(x > e\).

Hence f is increasing on \((e, \infty)\), and nowhere else: on \((0, 1)\) the logarithm is negative and on \((1, e)\) it lies between 0 and 1, so \(\log x - 1 < 0\) and f is decreasing on both of those stretches. The interval \([e, \infty)\) may equally be quoted, since \(f'\) vanishes only at the single endpoint \(x = e\).

rows.stem: If \((2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + \hat{k})\) and \((2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k})\) represent the sides \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) and \(\overrightarrow{AC}\) respectively of \(\Delta\) ABC, find the vector representing the median through A.
rows.solution:
The median through A joins A to D, the mid-point of the opposite side BC. Taking A as the origin of position vectors, D is the mid-point of B and C, so \(\overrightarrow{AD} = \dfrac{\overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{AC}}{2}\).

Here \(\overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{AC} = \left(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + \hat{k}\right) + \left(2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k}\right) = 4\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 0\hat{k}\).

Hence \(\overrightarrow{AD} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(4\hat{i} + 4\hat{j}\right) = 2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j}\), which is the vector representing the median through A. (Its length, if wanted, is \(\sqrt{4 + 4} = 2\sqrt{2}\).)

[CBSE marking scheme: in the printed subtraction the matrix \(4A\) is given a third row of \(\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 4 & 8 \end{bmatrix}\). That is \(4\) times \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), whereas the third row of A is \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) and so the third row of \(4A\) is \(\begin{bmatrix} 8 & 8 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\). Carried through as printed, the third row of the answer would be \(\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 4 & -4 \end{bmatrix}\) rather than zeros; the scheme's final null matrix is correct and only that one intermediate row is mistyped.]

First square A:
\(A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). Each diagonal entry is \(1 + 4 + 4 = 9\) and each off-diagonal entry is \(2 + 2 + 4 = 8\), so \(A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 8 & 8 \\ 8 & 9 & 8 \\ 8 & 8 & 9 \end{bmatrix}\).

Next, \(4A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 8 & 8 \\ 8 & 4 & 8 \\ 8 & 8 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(5I = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\).

Subtracting entry by entry, each diagonal entry gives \(9 - 4 - 5 = 0\) and each off-diagonal entry gives \(8 - 8 - 0 = 0\). Hence \(A^2 - 4A - 5I = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), the null matrix.

Incidentally this says \(A^2 = 4A + 5I\), so multiplying by \(A^{-1}\) gives \(A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{5}\left(A - 4I\right)\).

rows.subtopic: Graphical Solution and the Feasible Region
rows.stem:
Solve the following Linear Programming Problem graphically :

Minimize \(Z = 20x + 10y\)

subject to

\(x + 2y \leq 40\)

\(3x + y \geq 30\)

\(4x + 3y \geq 60\)

\(x, y \geq 0\)
rows.solution:
Draw the lines \(x + 2y = 40\), \(3x + y = 30\) and \(4x + 3y = 60\) in the first quadrant. Testing the origin, it satisfies \(x + 2y \le 40\) but fails both \(3x + y \ge 30\) and \(4x + 3y \ge 60\), so the feasible region lies below the first line and above the other two. It is a bounded quadrilateral.

Find the corner points by intersecting the boundary lines in pairs and keeping only the feasible ones.
On \(y = 0\): \(x + 2y = 40\) gives \((40, 0)\), which satisfies both remaining constraints; \(4x + 3y = 60\) gives \((15, 0)\), which satisfies them too; but \(3x + y = 30\) gives \((10, 0)\), where \(4x + 3y = 40 < 60\), so that point is rejected.
The lines \(3x + y = 30\) and \(4x + 3y = 60\) meet where \(y = 30 - 3x\) gives \(4x + 90 - 9x = 60\), so \(x = 6\) and \(y = 12\), that is \((6, 12)\); there \(x + 2y = 30 \le 40\), so it is feasible.
The lines \(3x + y = 30\) and \(x + 2y = 40\) meet where \(x = 40 - 2y\) gives \(120 - 6y + y = 30\), so \(y = 18\) and \(x = 4\), that is \((4, 18)\); there \(4x + 3y = 70 \ge 60\), so it is feasible.
On the y-axis, \((0, 20)\) and \((0, 30)\) both fail a constraint, so the region does not touch the y-axis.

The corner points are therefore \(A(40, 0)\), \(B(15, 0)\), \(C(6, 12)\) and \(D(4, 18)\).

Now evaluate \(Z = 20x + 10y\) at each: at \(A(40, 0)\), \(Z = 800\); at \(B(15, 0)\), \(Z = 300\); at \(C(6, 12)\), \(Z = 120 + 120 = 240\); at \(D(4, 18)\), \(Z = 80 + 180 = 260\).

The feasible region is bounded, so Z attains its minimum at a corner point. Hence the minimum value of Z is 240, at \(x = 6\), \(y = 12\).

rows.stem: Using integration, find the area of the region bounded by the curve \(y = x|x|\), x-axis, \(x = -2\) and \(x = 2\).
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: the two middle lines lose a sign. Having correctly written the area as \(-\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{0} x|x|\,dx + \int_{0}^{2} x|x|\,dx\), the scheme substitutes \(x|x| = -x^2\) on \([-2, 0]\) but keeps the minus with the integrand instead of cancelling it, printing \(\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{0}\left(-x^2\right)dx + \int_{0}^{2}x^2\,dx\) and then \(-\left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-2}^{0} + \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{2}\). Evaluated literally that chain gives \(-\frac{8}{3} + \frac{8}{3} = 0\), not the \(\frac{8}{3} + \frac{8}{3}\) printed beside it. The stated answer \(\frac{16}{3}\) is correct; it is the two intermediate lines that carry the stray minus.]

First unfold the modulus. For \(x \ge 0\), \(|x| = x\), so \(y = x|x| = x^2\); for \(x < 0\), \(|x| = -x\), so \(y = -x^2\). The curve is therefore the right half of the parabola \(y = x^2\) joined at the origin to the reflected left half \(y = -x^2\), rising through the first quadrant and dropping into the third. So on \([-2, 0]\) the curve lies BELOW the x-axis and on \([0, 2]\) it lies above it, and the two pieces must be integrated separately with the area of the lower piece taken positively.

Area \(= \displaystyle\int_{-2}^{0}\left|x|x|\right|dx + \int_{0}^{2}\left|x|x|\right|dx = \int_{-2}^{0} x^2\,dx + \int_{0}^{2} x^2\,dx\), since \(\left|-x^2\right| = x^2\).

Now \(\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{0} x^2\,dx = \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-2}^{0} = 0 - \left(-\dfrac{8}{3}\right) = \dfrac{8}{3}\) and \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} x^2\,dx = \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{2} = \dfrac{8}{3}\).

Hence the required area is \(\dfrac{8}{3} + \dfrac{8}{3} = \dfrac{16}{3}\) square units.

The same answer follows in one line from symmetry: \(y = x|x|\) is an odd function, so the two pieces are congruent and the area is \(2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} x^2\,dx = 2 \times \dfrac{8}{3} = \dfrac{16}{3}\) square units — the alternative approach the scheme itself notes.

rows.subtopic: Equation of a Line in Space
rows.stem: Find the vector and cartesian equations of the line passing through the point of intersection of the lines \(\vec{r} = (\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k}) + \lambda(3\hat{i} - \hat{j})\) and \(\vec{r} = (4\hat{i} - \hat{k}) + \mu(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{k})\) and parallel to the line \(\dfrac{x - 1}{-2} = \dfrac{7 - y}{-3} = z\).
rows.solution:
Step 1 — find where the two lines meet. A general point on \(\vec{r} = \left(\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k}\right) + \lambda\left(3\hat{i} - \hat{j}\right)\) is \(P(3\lambda + 1,\; 1 - \lambda,\; -1)\), and a general point on \(\vec{r} = \left(4\hat{i} - \hat{k}\right) + \mu\left(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{k}\right)\) is \(Q(2\mu + 4,\; 0,\; 3\mu - 1)\).

Equating the y-coordinates gives \(1 - \lambda = 0\), so \(\lambda = 1\); equating the z-coordinates gives \(3\mu - 1 = -1\), so \(\mu = 0\). These must also be consistent with the x-coordinates, and they are: \(3(1) + 1 = 4\) and \(2(0) + 4 = 4\). So the lines do intersect, at the point \((4, 0, -1)\).

Step 2 — find the required direction. The line \(\dfrac{x - 1}{-2} = \dfrac{7 - y}{-3} = z\) must first be put in standard symmetric form: \(\dfrac{7 - y}{-3} = \dfrac{y - 7}{3}\), so the line is \(\dfrac{x - 1}{-2} = \dfrac{y - 7}{3} = \dfrac{z - 0}{1}\) and its direction ratios are \(\langle -2, 3, 1 \rangle\). A line parallel to it has the same direction ratios.

Step 3 — write the required line through \((4, 0, -1)\) with direction ratios \(\langle -2, 3, 1 \rangle\).

Vector form: \(\vec{r} = \left(4\hat{i} - \hat{k}\right) + \omega\left(-2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + \hat{k}\right)\), where \(\omega\) is a scalar parameter.

Cartesian form: \(\dfrac{x - 4}{-2} = \dfrac{y}{3} = \dfrac{z + 1}{1}\).
